{{Short description|Mathematical object}}
[[File:Torus-spir.svg|thumb|Spiric sections as planar sections of a torus]]
In [[geometry]], a '''spiric section''', sometimes called a '''spiric of Perseus''', is a quartic [[plane curve]] defined by equations of the form

:<math>(x^2+y^2)^2=dx^2+ey^2+f. \, </math>

Equivalently, spiric sections can be defined as [[Circular algebraic curve|bicircular]] quartic curves that are symmetric with respect to the ''x'' and ''y''-axes. Spiric sections are included in the family of [[toric section]]s and include the family of [[hippopede]]s and the family of [[Cassini oval]]s. The name is from σπειρα meaning "torus" in ancient Greek.<ref>{{cite book
 | last1 = Brieskorn | first1 = Egbert |author-link=Egbert Brieskorn
 | last2 = Knörrer | first2 = Horst |author2-link=Horst Knörrer
 | translator-last = Stillwell | translator-first = John
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-0348-5097-1
 | isbn = 978-3-0348-0492-9
 | mr = 2975988
 | page = 16
 | publisher = Birkhäuser/Springer Basel AG
 | series = Modern Birkhäuser Classics
 | title = Plane algebraic curves
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=qsDzBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA16
 | year = 1986}} The word ''σπειρα'' originally meant a coil of rope, and came to refer to the base of a column, which for certain orders of column was shaped as a torus: see {{cite book|contribution=Spira|url=https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/secondary/SMIGRA*/Spira.html|first=James|last=Yates|title=A Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities|publisher=John Murray|location=London|year=1875|editor-first=William|editor-last=Smith}}</ref>

A spiric section is sometimes defined as the curve of intersection of a [[torus]] and a plane parallel to its [[rotational symmetry]] axis. However, this definition does not include all of the curves given by the previous definition unless [[Imaginary number|imaginary]] planes are allowed.

Spiric sections were first described by the ancient Greek  geometer [[Perseus (geometer)|Perseus]] in roughly 150 BC, and are assumed to be the first toric sections to be described. The name ''spiric'' is due to the ancient notation ''spira'' of a torus.,<ref>John Stillwell: ''Mathematics and Its History'', Springer-Verlag, 2010, {{isbn|978-1-4419-6053-5}}, p. 33.</ref><ref>[[Wilbur Knorr|Wilbur R. Knorr]]: ''[[The Ancient Tradition of Geometric Problems]]'', Dover-Publ., New York, 1993, {{isbn|0-486-67532-7}}, p. 268 .</ref>

==Equations==
[[Image:Spiric section.svg|thumb|right|''a''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, ''b''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, ''c''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0,&nbsp;0.8,&nbsp;1]]
Start with the usual equation for the torus:

:<math>(x^2+y^2+z^2+b^2-a^2)^2 = 4b^2(x^2+y^2). \, </math>

Interchanging ''y'' and ''z'' so that the axis of revolution is now on the ''xy''-plane, and setting ''z''=''c'' to find the curve of intersection gives

:<math>(x^2+y^2-a^2+b^2+c^2)^2 = 4b^2(x^2+c^2). \, </math>

In this formula, the [[torus]] is formed by rotating a circle of radius ''a'' with its center following another circle of radius ''b'' (not necessarily larger than ''a'', self-intersection is permitted).  The parameter ''c'' is the distance from the intersecting plane to the axis of revolution.  There are no spiric sections with ''c''&nbsp;>&nbsp;''b''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''a'', since there is no intersection; the plane is too far away from the torus to intersect it.

Expanding the equation gives the form seen in the definition

:<math>(x^2+y^2)^2=dx^2+ey^2+f \, </math>

where

:<math>d=2(a^2+b^2-c^2),\ e=2(a^2-b^2-c^2),\ f=-(a^4+b^4+c^4-2a^2b^2-2a^2c^2-2b^2c^2). \, </math>

In [[polar coordinates]] this becomes

:<math>(r^2-a^2+b^2+c^2)^2 = 4b^2(r^2\cos^2\theta+c^2) \, </math>

or

:<math>r^4=r^2(d\cos^2\theta+e\sin^2\theta)+f. </math>
[[File:Torus-spind-spir.svg|thumb|Spiric sections on a spindle torus]]

==  Spiric sections on a spindle torus ==
Spiric sections on a spindle torus, whose planes intersect the spindle (inner part), consist of an outer and an inner curve (s. picture).

== Spiric sections as isoptics ==
[[Orthoptic (geometry)|Isoptic]]s of ellipses and hyperbolas are spiric sections. (S. also weblink ''The Mathematics Enthusiast''.)

==Examples of spiric sections==
Examples include the [[hippopede]] and the [[Cassini oval]] and their relatives, such as the [[lemniscate of Bernoulli]].  The [[Cassini oval]] has the remarkable property that the ''product'' of distances to two foci are constant.  For comparison, the sum is constant in [[ellipse]]s, the difference is constant in [[hyperbola]]e and the ratio is constant in [[circle]]s.
